extracted.intended_audience: NPS employees, park staff, and fire/emergency management personnel who want to become Public Information Officers
extracted.subtask_short: becoming an NPS public information officer
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for NPS staff on the training, taskbooks, certification, physical requirements, and administrative steps needed to qualify and serve as a Public Information Officer (PIO) within the Incident Command System for wildland fire and other incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: PIO role and responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: A PIO is responsible for the formulation and release of information about the incident to the news media, local communities, incident personnel, the incident management team, other agencies and organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As you progress you may become a lead public information officer, responsible for management of other PIOs assigned to the incident. PIOs set up fire information posts and coordinate communications for incidents and events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incident Command System (ICS) reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The public information officer reports to the incident commander, who in turn reports to the agency or jurisdictions responsible for the incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good overview of ICS is provided in the independent study course 'Introduction to ICS (ICS-100)'. PIO duties should be understood in the context of ICS structure and chains of command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility and core skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Technically, anyone can become a PIO, but it does require good interpersonal communication skills and writing skills to meet the needs of the position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Candidates should assess and develop both interpersonal and written communication abilities before pursuing taskbooks or assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: PIO qualification levels
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three levels of public information officer positions: PIO Technician (PIOT), PIO3 (Type 3), and PIO Complex (PIOC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can begin locally at PIOT by taking online courses (no taskbook requirement). As you progress, work becomes more complex up to the PIOC level. Taskbooks and certification requirements differ by level.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to start the certification process
rubrics_metrics.description: First, discuss your interest with your supervisor. Then, contact your local fire or emergency management officer who can initiate your taskbook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your home unit must initiate the position taskbook; supervisors and local officers are the administrative starting points to begin training and tracking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and qualification pathways (four avenues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Training and qualifications are completed through four avenues: Training Courses; Position Taskbooks; Job Aids; Agency Certification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training Courses provide background knowledge; Position Taskbooks contain required tasks; Job Aids provide ready reference; Agency Certification documents that the individual is qualified and is the employing agency's responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position taskbooks availability and initiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Position taskbooks are available on the National Wildfire Coordinating Group positions catalog. Your home unit must initiate the taskbook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search the NWCG positions catalog for 'Public Information Officer' to find the appropriate PIO taskbooks and qualifications. Taskbooks are the record of required tasks to be signed off.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIMS Wildland Fire Qualification System Guide compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: PIOs (who work fire and other events) are certified through the completion of requirements listed in the NIMS Wildland Fire Qualification System Guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the NIMS guide for specific qualification criteria and certification pathways applicable to PIO positions on fire incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training delivery standards and course access
rubrics_metrics.description: Some training is available online for free; other courses are classroom only. See the NWCG Standards for Course Delivery for more details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check locally with your fire management officer or the Wildland Fire Learning Portal for schedules. If needed, consider NPS training grants and the Wildland Fire Workforce Development Grant Program for funding travel/tuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical fitness requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically, a PIO has no physical fitness requirements to hold that position, UNLESS that PIO will be expected to visit the fireline to take photos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If expected to visit the fireline a light duty work capacity test may be required. Confirm assignment-specific physical expectations before deploying to line operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire shelter deployment requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Another physical requirement includes demonstration that you can deploy, get in, and stay inside a fire shelter for a specified duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a demonstrable capability required for personnel who will operate in or near fireline environments; training and practice opportunities should be sought out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate submission and initial qualification cards
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have taken the initial online training for PIOT, you will turn your certificates in to your training officer or supervisor to be reviewed to receive a qualification card for PIOT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no experience necessary to become a PIOT. After turning in certificates and meeting requirements you receive a qualification card stating your current trainee or qualified status (e.g., PIO3(t), PIOC(t)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final certification, IQCS (Red Card), and IROC registration
rubrics_metrics.description: When any taskbook is completed, your home unit will finalize your certification. You should receive an Incident Qualifications and Certification System card (IQCS card or Red Card) to state that you are qualified as a PIO; you must also be registered in the Interagency Resource Ordering Capability (IROC) system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IQCS/Red Card is required to go on the fireline on incidents. Check with your park or regional fire management officer for issuance and with unit protocol for being added to IROC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working as a trainee and required currency to deploy
rubrics_metrics.description: You can work as a trainee as long as you have a red card, an initiated taskbook and an annual refresher. Training and taskbook must be completed to be fully qualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trainee status allows participation but full qualification requires taskbook completion and agency sign-off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taskbook and currency expiration rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Taskbooks expire three years from the date the first task in the taskbook is signed off. PIOs must have an assignment at least once every five years to maintain currency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor dates closely; plan assignments and refreshers to avoid lapses in qualifications and to maintain eligibility for deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record-keeping and availability notifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularly update your incident experience, training, and taskbook records with your fire program management assistant or dispatch with the IQCS update form. Once you have supervisor approval, let your local dispatch office know when you are available locally, regionally, or nationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining up-to-date records and notifying dispatch of availability are administrative requirements to be considered for incident assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social media and communication tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media is a tool often used by public information officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PIOs should be familiar with social media as part of their communications toolkit and be able to incorporate it appropriately into incident information strategies.
